## Pitch is an address, and addresses do arithmetic

You can write a pitch as `:c4`, which reads nicely and pairs a note name with a
register. Inside the program it isn't a name at all. `note(:c4)` gives you 60,
and once pitch is an integer, transformations that sound wildly different turn
into ordinary operations on arrays.

This program takes five note symbols, converts them straight away, and builds
two relatives of the original before anything sounds. `reverse` gives you a
retrograde by changing order. Subtracting around an axis gives you an inversion
by changing direction, reflecting every interval above the first E the same
distance below it.

Listen to all three as a family. The rhythm never moves and they share the same
source array, but each transformation protects something different. Retrograde
keeps the pitches and reverses their order. Inversion keeps the interval sizes
and flips their sign.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 104
use_synth :piano

original = [:e4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :a4].map { |name| note(name) }
retrograde = original.reverse
axis = original.first
inversion = original.map { |pitch| axis - (pitch - axis) }

define :play_phrase do |pitches, duration|
  pitches.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
  sleep 1
end

play_phrase original, 0.5
play_phrase retrograde, 0.5
play_phrase inversion, 0.5
puts midi_to_hz(original.first)
```

The first phrase climbs from E and bends back from B. The retrograde opens on
what used to be the last note and walks the array backwards. The inversion also
opens on E, but everything that rose now falls. That one-beat gap after each
form matters: it lets one contour clear your ear before the next arrives.

## Three edits, one at a time

1. Add `12` to every value in `original`. Every pitch jumps an octave while the
   distances between neighbours stay put, so you get an identical contour in a
   brighter register.

2. Restore it, then set `axis` to `note(:b3)`. Reflection still preserves
   interval sizes, but a lower mirror drops the whole inverted phrase into a new
   range. Print the array before you listen, and check the numbers against the
   shape you hear.

3. Restore the program again. Print `midi_to_hz(original.first)`, feed that
   frequency back through `hz_to_midi`, and compare with the integer you
   started from. What does that round trip tell you about where the keyboard
   address ends and physical frequency begins?

Keep those edits separate. Move the axis and the register together and the
lower result stops telling you which operation caused it.

## Why arithmetic works on pitch

Adjacent MIDI integers sit one semitone apart, so addition is transposition.
`+ 12` is an octave up, `+ 7` is an equal-tempered fifth. The step size is
uniform right across the range, which is exactly what makes a pitch array
pleasant to inspect and transform.

Inversion needs a little more structure. For each pitch, `pitch - axis` is the
signed distance from the mirror note, and subtracting that distance from the
axis lands you on the far side. Three semitones above E becomes three semitones
below E. The sign flips, the magnitude doesn't.

Retrograde answers a different question, because it leaves every value alone and
changes only when each one happens. Given `[64, 67, 69]`, its retrograde is
`[69, 67, 64]` and its inversion around 64 is `[64, 61, 59]`. Those two are much
easier to tell apart in the log than on a first hearing, so keep it visible.

Numbers aren't the whole story. `midi_to_hz` crosses from a symbolic keyboard
address to a physical frequency and `hz_to_midi` crosses back, and later lessons
will hang on to note spellings when the names carry harmonic meaning. Here,
integers are the right working representation because arithmetic is the subject.

One more thing to expect: an inverted phrase can fall right out of the useful
range of your synth. That's an audible consequence of correct arithmetic, not a
broken formula. Print the minimum and maximum of each form before playback, and
if a result needs relocating, transpose the whole thing by twelve semitones.
Clipping the one offending note would wreck the interval pattern that inversion
exists to preserve.

[Lesson 3](03-time-beats-seconds.qmd) leaves these arrays completely alone and changes their tempo. That
separation is worth as much as this one: pitch data survives a new rate the same
way this phrase survived reversal and reflection.

## Take it further

Build a transposed form five semitones up, then play four versions in this
order: original, transposition, retrograde, inversion. Reuse `play_phrase`
instead of copying its loop, and print each array immediately before it sounds.
Your log becomes a compact numeric score you can read along with.

Use one duration and one renderer throughout, so order, direction and register
stay the only audible variables. Check the arrays before you trust your ears:
transposition adds five to everything, retrograde holds the same items in
reverse, and inversion preserves each distance from the axis with the sign
flipped. Then listen in Sonic Pi 5. A correct array proves the transformation
happened. Only listening tells you whether the result still has a clear shape in
the register it landed in.
